title: John Oliver Embarrasses Trump Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy Over ‘Godawful’ YouTube Reality Show and ‘Real World’ Past
description:
John Oliver is an outspoken fan of reality TV — but not this former “Real World” star.

	On Sunday’s “Last Week Tonight,” the political pundit took
body:
John Oliver is an outspoken fan of reality TV — but not this former “Real World” star.

	On Sunday’s “Last Week Tonight,” the political pundit took aim squarely at Sean Duffy, President Trump’s Secretary of Transportation and former congressman and “The Real World: Boston” cast member. You see, on Wednesday, Duffy dropped all six episodes of “The Great American Road Trip” to YouTube. Though it bills itself as a reality show celebrating America’s 250th anniversary, its travel and its people, as Oliver pointed out, “It’s basically just an expensively-produced test run of a Duffy family reality show with each episode featuring a bare minimum about travel or America but a ton of manufactured reality-TV drama around the Duffy’s doing stuff like planning a family party or, over the course of several episodes, watching their daughter decide which college she’ll attend.” (Duffy’s wife is Fox News contributor Rachel Campos-Duffy, who he met on MTV’s “Road Rules: All Stars.”)
	

	In a clip from the show that was widely mocked online, while discussing whether his daughter can go to Harvard, Duffy remarked, “If I send you there, I think what happens is they have professionalized figuring out how they can take good, young girls like you and, I think, corrupt their minds.”


	“What the fuck are you talking about?” exclaimed Oliver. “First, this was supposed to be a road trip — why are we still in your kitchen? Second, is there anything less relatable than a family whose conflict is, how do I tell my daughter she can’t go to Harvard because we did too good of a job raising her?”
	

	Duffy claimed that the show was shot over seven months and that no taxpayer money was used; rather, the show was funded by the independent company Great American Road Trip Inc., which listed 17 sponsors, Boeing, Toyota, Shell and United Airlines among them, all companies overseen and regulated by Duffy’s Department of Transportation.

	“That’s not great! The only worse answer to ‘Who paid for this?’ than ‘The American taxpayer’ is ‘a bunch of companies I oversee and regulate,’” cracked Oliver.

	And, when Duffy was pressed about the conflict of interest in Congress, he replied, “Don’t you want to celebrate America?” adding, “It’s our birthday!”

	“It’s our birthday? You sound like a fucking child!” exclaimed Oliver. “You do get that just because it’s America’s birthday doesn’t mean you get to do an ethics violation, right? Grow up, Sean!”

	The show was supposed to come out in June but Duffy said it needed to be re-edited so it abided by ethics rules. And Duffy, of course, is a reality-TV veteran.

	“[Duffy] has long loved being on camera. He was actually on ‘The Real World: Boston’ in the late-90s, where he presented himself as deeply horny,” explained Oliver. “In his audition, he reportedly said that he wanted to be on the show because of his interest in ‘cute girls,’ and when asked by a producer how many times he’d had sex in the last six months, he — and I’m quoting here — flashed a big smile and said, ‘Three times. Three different individuals, yeah. And three different times,’ adding, ‘I’m sort of starving right now, guys.’”

	Cue Oliver: “And I’ve got to say: I had sex with three different women, none of whom were interested in an encore, says a lot more about you than I think you wanted to reveal there.”

	What’s worse, during his time on “The Real World: Boston,” Duffy “got attention for annoying the fuck out of his Black castmate Kameelah, who he fought with over affirmative action, complaining he would have gotten into a better college ‘if I were a Black male,’ and at another point, ‘compared [her] to Adolf Hitler while accusing her of reverse racism,’” Oliver offered.  

	As for “The Great American Road Trip,” its YouTube views are dwindling in the thousands and its YouTube page has less than 3K subscribers at time of writing.
	

	“Everyone involved in ‘The Great American Road Trip’ seems like they’d rather sweep it under the rug,” Oliver maintained. “Since it came out, the Duffy’s have barely promoted the show and the Department of Transportation hasn’t posted about it at all… But even if everyone involved wants to move on and act like it never happened, I’m not sure the rest of us should, because the appearance of a conflict of interest here is not going to go away.”

	Oliver then cited how the Department of Transportation has two open investigations into Waymo, which is featured in the series, including for striking a child in the vicinity of a school.

	“Having watched all three hours of this godawful show, from gender reveals to the Duffy’s renewing their vows for no clear reason, it feels less like the country’s been taken on a road trip by Sean Duffy and a lot more like we’ve all been taken for a fucking ride,” he concluded.

schema.headline: John Oliver Embarrasses Trump Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy Over ‘Godawful’ YouTube Reality Show and ‘Real World’ Past

title: Katseye Earns First No. 1 on Albums Chart; Phoebe Bridgers Debuts at No. 2
description:
Katseye has scored their first No. 1 on the Billboard 200 as their latest project “Wild” debuts atop the list.

	“Wild,” the five-track offering led
body:
Katseye has scored their first No. 1 on the Billboard 200 as their latest project “Wild” debuts atop the list.

	“Wild,” the five-track offering led by the singles “Pinky Up” and “Hootie Frutti,” bows at the chart’s summit with 170,000 equivalent album units, marking their biggest week by that metric and by pure album sales with 145,000. Katseye‘s latest is the fourth No. 1 album by an all-woman group this decade after Twice’s “With You-th,” NewJeans’ “2nd EP ‘Get Up'” and Blackpink’s “Born Pink.” It also has the largest pure album sales week for an all-woman group in more than three years.
	

	Katseye previously reached a high of No. 4 on the Billboard 200 with 2025’s “Beautiful Chaos.” Their debut, “SIS (Soft Is Strong),” was released in 2024 and peaked at No. 98.


	Behind “Wild” sits Phoebe Bridgers‘ “Lost Weekend,” bowing at No. 2 with 118,000 equivalent album units earned. It marks her first solo project to reach the top 10 and becomes her best week ever by units. The singer-songwriter previously made the top 10 on the Billboard 200 with Boygenius, her trio with Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker, when their 2023 album “The Record” peaked at No. 4.

	Stray Kids’ “This & That,” which debuted at No. 1 last week, slides to No. 3, followed by Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” at No. 4 and Ella Langley’s “Dandelion” at No. 5.

	Rounding out the rest of the top 10 are Morgan Wallen’s “I’m the Problem” (No. 6), Ariana Grande’s “Petal” (No. 8), Drake’s “Iceman” (No. 9) and Olivia Dean’s “The Art of Loving” (No. 10).

schema.headline: Katseye Earns First No. 1 on Albums Chart; Phoebe Bridgers Debuts at No. 2

title: Ridley Scott Says ‘I’m Not a Filmmaker, I’m an Influencer’
description:
Ridley Scott recently told The Times of London that he sees himself not as a “filmmaker,” but as an “influencer.”

	“Every time, you are vulnerable,
body:
Ridley Scott recently told The Times of London that he sees himself not as a “filmmaker,” but as an “influencer.”

	“Every time, you are vulnerable,” Scott said when asked to identify a through line in his work. “Also, I never want to repeat myself and all my films have been on the money. I’ve been ahead of the game frequently and, if you’re ahead of the game, you’re an influencer. So I’m not a filmmaker, I’m an influencer.”
	

	Scott, a three-time Oscar-nominated director, has certainly flexed his influence throughout his years in Hollywood with immortal classics like “Blade Runner,” “Alien,” “Thelma & Louise,” and “Gladiator.” Earlier in the sit-down, he noted there are things he has yet to cross off his career checklist.


	“I’ve never done a Western,” he said. “I have cast Hugh Jackman for my ‘Treasure Island’ adaptation. I want to do a musical and, also, have a marvelous film about the African elephant.”

	Scott’s next film is “The Dog Stars” with Jacob Elordi, Margaret Qualley and Josh Brolin. He deemed his leading man Elordi “a big star” and said they “got on great.” He went on to imply that the reason he directed “The Dog Stars” was because he sensed tedious sameness in the type of stories coming out of Hollywood.

	“Look, everything now is about a murdered girl in the woods, or an FBI agent who is better than anyone else — or a superhero,” Scott said. “Fuck me! There have to be other stories to tell.”

	Scott will soon receive an honorary Oscar at November’s Governors Awards. Other recipients include Glenn Close and Disney’s first Black animator, Floyd Norman.

schema.headline: Ridley Scott Says ‘I’m Not a Filmmaker, I’m an Influencer’

title: ‘Sentimental Value’ Star Anders Danielsen Lie and Anne Marie Ottersen Inducted Into the Haugesund Walk of Fame: ‘It Feels Full Circle’
description:
Norwegian actors Anders Danielsen Lie and Anne Marie Ottersen were inducted into the Haugesund Walk of Fame.. 

	The unveiling taking  place during
body:
Norwegian actors Anders Danielsen Lie and Anne Marie Ottersen were inducted into the Haugesund Walk of Fame.. 

	The unveiling taking  place during the first weekend of this year’s Norwegian Intl. Film Festival Haugesund,  Danielsen Lie and Ottersen were recognized for contributing to “building the professionalism and high standards of Norway’s acting community, both on the theatre stage and in the film and television industry,” noted the committee. They join the ranks of Liv Ullmann, Pål Sverre Hagen and Renate Reinsve.
	

	“Do I look back? I haven’t had much time to reflect on this yet because my life is so hectic at the moment. But I do remember releasing [his 1990 acting debut] ‘Herman’ in Haugesund more than 30 years ago, so it feels full circle to receive this honor here,” Anders Danielsen Lie told Variety.


	“I think I dreamed of becoming a great actor when I was a young adult, but I abandoned that dream when I started med school. It was Joachim Trier’s first film that restarted my career,” he said.  

	“I think there are several ‘before’ and ‘after’ moments in my career, with the first being ‘Reprise’. If it weren’t for that film, I would never have worked as an actor.”

	While “Oslo, August 31st” was probably “the biggest turning point” in his career, smash hits “The Worst Person in the World” and “Sentimental Value” – also directed by Trier – introduced him to an even bigger audience. 

	“It’s always hard to say exactly why a film is loved by the audience, but they both tell stories that are relatable to many people. They are very entertaining films, but they also have an almost therapeutic quality to them,” he noted, adding: “I’m a bit surprised I have an international career, because I’ve always been ambivalent about acting – but hopefully that adds an extra layer of complexity to my work!” 
	

	Following “Sentimental Value’s” Oscar win – and nine nominations – Norwegian films definitely have an international momentum at the moment, he noted. 

	“I think there are several reasons for that. One is that we have great funding opportunities for films with limited commercial potential. I think Norwegian cinema as a whole has much more self-confidence now, which has been built up over many years. What we see now is the end result of a long evolution.” 

	Anne Marie Ottersen was surprised by the recognition. 

	“It was totally unexpected, but [it made me] very happy. In theater, most of what we do is gone with the wind once the performance is over. But now I’m written in stone, and that will last almost forever,” she said. 

	Ottersen joined the National Theatre in 1970, and won the Amanda Award for “Wives – Ten Years Later.” Her latest film, “The Pension Heist” directed by Gunnbjörg Gunnarsdóttir, will be released in October.  

	“The best thing I can say about my career is that I have been lucky to do so many different things. There have been difficult periods, of course, but I have the best job in the world, and I’m still working. I’m so happy about that.”

	The Walk of Fame was established in 2015, when actors Kristoffer Joner and Ane Dahl Torp became the first recipients.

	The Norwegian Intl. Film Festival Haugesund runs Aug. 22-28.

schema.headline: ‘Sentimental Value’ Star Anders Danielsen Lie and Anne Marie Ottersen Inducted Into the Haugesund Walk of Fame: ‘It Feels Full Circle’

title: Martin Short Gets Honest: What It’s Like to Be All Over the Emmy Race, Thanks to Three Very Different Projects
description: Martin Short is having quite a unique Emmy season, and he knows it. His name is all over this year’s nominations, via three very distinct projects:
body:
Martin Short is having quite a unique Emmy season, and he knows it. His name is all over this year’s nominations, via three very distinct projects: As an actor, he’s nominated for outstanding comedy lead via Hulu’s “Only Murders in the Building.” (He also has a comedy series nom for the show as an executive producer.) As a game show host, he landed a nod for ABC’s “Match Game.” And then he’s the subject of director Lawrence Kasdan’s Netflix documentary “Marty, Life Is Short,” which scored three noms this year.
	

	Short isn’t actually a part of the production team on “Marty, Life Is Short,” so he won’t get an Emmy if it wins for outstanding documentary or nonfiction special. But he gave the film, and Kasdan — whom he’s known for 40 years — his full support.


	“[Kasdan] phoned and said that he and Ron Howard and Imagine would love to do this documentary on me, and I kind of went, ‘I don’t know, I’ve written a book, I’m Canadian, we’re a little more reserved, let me think about it,’” Short says. Kasdan then left an eight-minute message explaining why Short’s story — about celebrating life, using humor to work through grief and more — was an important one to share.

	Kasdan also knew Short had a ton of material to mine: “Through all these years, I’ve always had a camcorder,” Short says. “With all my kids, I would just film. And I’d have them transferred to DVD. Because of my relationship and trust with him, I was able to take these shelves of movies and just say, ‘here you go.’”

	Not only that, but Steven Spielberg also sent over a ton of home movies he had made with Short in them. “So Larry had a great little treasure trove of stuff,” Short says.
	

	When Short’s daughter Katherine died in February, Kasdan told the star that Netflix could hold back the documentary’s release if the star wasn’t comfortable with it at that moment. But Short told them that they should proceed.

	“We met at his home a few weeks after, and he said, ‘Netflix will do whatever you want and I will do whatever you want,’” Short says. “And I thought, this really could be called ‘Love, Loss and Survival.’ As I’ve said in the past, my daughter had mental health struggles. And it’s a disease. Some diseases are terminal, whether they’re cancer or mental health. And so, I said, ‘I think we should proceed.’ And he said, ‘I think we should too.’”

	And since the film premiered globally in May, Short says he’s heard from many folks on how they appreciated seeing how he navigated through such tremendous loss in his life.

	Coincidentally, Short is also seen quite a bit in the Amazon doc “John Candy: I Like Me,” about his pal and “SCTV” co-star, which is competing against “Marty, Life Is Short” in this year’s Emmys documentary or nonfiction special category. Short says it was Candy who inspired him to start his home video habit. “In 1981, I got a VHS machine, and I went, ‘what am I doing? John has Betamax. We can’t exchange movies! So I went back and traded my VHS for Beta. You don’t even want to know my LaserDisc collection.”

	As for “Match Game,” Short says there are no future seasons in the works for him, but “never say never.” And he’s tightlipped on what to expect for next season’s “Only Murders” other than its move to London and a new batch of A-list guest stars.

	But he’ll be back in L.A. next month for sure, given his tremendous showing as an Emmy nominee. “Let’s do the cliché, it’s a tremendous honor to be recognized by your peers,” he says. Then he adds with a smile, “I am Mr. Emmy this year!”

schema.headline: Martin Short Gets Honest: What It’s Like to Be All Over the Emmy Race, Thanks to Three Very Different Projects

title: Mark Ruffalo Called Out Over ‘Extremist and Antisemitic Messaging’ by Simon Wiesenthal Center, Creative Communities For Peace
description:
Two prominent Jewish advocacy groups have called out Mark Ruffalo for spreading “antisemitic tropes.”

	“Words matter, and so does the willingness t
body:
Two prominent Jewish advocacy groups have called out Mark Ruffalo for spreading “antisemitic tropes.”

	“Words matter, and so does the willingness to draw a line when legitimate debate gives way to antisemitic tropes,” said Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center. 

	“We commend Paramount for speaking clearly and refusing to allow prejudice to masquerade as political or corporate criticism. At a time when antisemitism is too often minimized, rationalized, or repackaged in more socially acceptable language, this kind of moral clarity matters.”
	

	Ari Ingel, executive director of Creative Community for Peace, also said in a statement: “Mark Ruffalo’s rhetoric has increasingly crossed the line from criticism of Israel into extremist and antisemitic messaging.”


	Their intervention comes after Paramount issued a rare statement of condemnation against Ruffalo on Friday, in which the company said it is “troubled when antisemitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute.”

	That statement was in response to the actor’s Instagram re-posting of a year-old video clip featuring Jewish Paramount Skydance board member Safra Catz speaking on a panel. In text accompanying the clip he told his 20 million Instagram followers it showed Catz “revelling” in a “genocide” powered by tech company Oracle, understood to be a tacit reference to the Israel-Hamas conflict.

	Catz is the former CEO of Oracle, which was co-founded by Larry Ellison, father of Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison.

	Paramount Skydance is in the process of acquiring Warner Bros. Discovery. Ruffalo has been one of the most vocal critics of the deal.
	

	In his latest social media screed, Ruffalo said Larry Ellison was funding his son’s acquisition of Warner and that he would own “most of” the company if the deal, which is currently mired in legal tangling with 12 state attorneys general, went through.

	Larry Ellison has reportedly committed up to $46.7 billion of the $111 billion deal, with a trio of Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds, comprised of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi, also committing at least $24 billion.

	Ruffalo, who is believed to have earned millions from his role as Hulk in the Marvel films, also called Ellison Sr. a “classic Oligarch” who is “crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance” in his commentary. He also accused the Ellisons of “powering some of the most destructive and inhuman forces in the world.”

	After Paramount issued its statement condemning his post, the Marvel actor fired back on X, saying the accusation of antisemitism “is appalling and fundamentally dishonest.”

	However, at least two Jewish orgs appear to agree with Paramount’s assessment. “Invoking Israel in an issue where it is completely irrelevant is a textbook case of obsession and demonization,” Berk, the Simon Wiesenthal Center CEO, continued in his statement. “Paramount was right to call it out. More leaders and institutions should have the courage to call antisemitism what it is, regardless of who is spreading it.”

	Meanwhile CCFP’s Ingel, noted: “Ruffalo now says accusations of antisemitism against him are ‘fundamentally dishonest.’ Intent does not erase impact. Repeatedly amplifying inflammatory falsehoods and rhetoric that mirrors historic antisemitic tropes helps normalize the violent anti-Jewish hatred we are seeing take hold once again around the world, regardless of how he chooses to describe his own motives.”

schema.headline: Mark Ruffalo Called Out Over ‘Extremist and Antisemitic Messaging’ by Simon Wiesenthal Center, Creative Communities For Peace

title: Shelley Fabares, ‘Coach’ and ‘The Donna Reed Show’ Star, Dies at 82
description:
Shelley Fabares, the star of the classic sitcoms “The Donna Reed Show” and “Coach,” died on Saturday in Los Angeles. She was 82.

	Fabares’ family s
body:
Shelley Fabares, the star of the classic sitcoms “The Donna Reed Show” and “Coach,” died on Saturday in Los Angeles. She was 82.

	Fabares’ family said in a statement, “We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday lives. We are heartbroken by her loss, yet profoundly grateful for the years we shared with her and for the joy, compassion, and love she brought to so many. We ask that our family’s privacy be respected as we grieve. We take comfort in knowing that Shelley’s work and the memories she created with those who loved her will continue to live on.”
	

	Fabares starred as the Stone family daughter Mary in “The Donna Reed Show,” which ran on ABC for 275 episodes from 1958 to 1966. Fabares appeared in 192 episodes and left the series in 1965. On ABC’s “Coach,” which ranf or 199 episodes from 1989 to 1997, she played Christine Armstrong, a TV news anchor and the romantic interest of Craig T. Nelson’s college football coach Hayden Fox. She earned two Emmy nominations, in 1993 and 1994, for supporting comedy actress for her work on the series.


	Fabares also had a brief career as a singer during her time on “The Donna Reed Show,” notching a No.1 hit with her 1961 track “Johnny Angel.” She parlayed her TV fame into a series of teen-centric B-movie romps including opposite Fabian and Tab Hunter in 1964’s “Ride the Wild Surf,” and she co-starred with Elvis Presley in three films, 1965’s “Girl Happy,” 1966’s “Spinout!” and 1967’s “Clambake.”

	Some of Fabares’ other TV credits include “The Little People,” “Forever Fernwood,” “The Practice,” “Hello, Larry,” “Highcliffe Manor,” “Fantasy Island,” “One Day at a Time” and “The Love Boat.” She had a key role on one of the most lauded TV movies of the 1970s, ABC’s “Brian’s Song,” starring James Caan and Billy Dee Williams in the true story of the friendship between two NFL players as one of them faces terminal cancer. Fabares played Joy Piccolo, the wife of Caan’s Brian Piccolo.
	

	Fabares was born in Santa Monica, Calif. in 1944 and grew up around Hollywood. Her mother, Elsa, started her modeling career at a young age, which led to roles on TV. Fabares’ aunt, Nanette Fabray, was a well-known Broadway star and film supporting player who also transitioned to TV roles. Among Fabares’ early TV breaks was a two-episode stint on “The Loretta Young Show” in 1954. Her first major film credit came in a supporting role in the 1956 Rock Hudson drama “Never Say Goodbye,” for Universal International.

	Fabares was briefly married to influential music and movie producer Lou Adler in the mid-1960s. In 1984, Fabares married actor Mike Farrell, known for his long run on the CBS comedy “MASH.” In the 1980s and ’90s, Farrell and Fabares were active in numerous political and social causes, including protesting U.S. activities in Central America and supporting the anti-nuclear movement that took root in Southern California in the late 1970s.

	Like Farrell, Fabares was active behind the scenes on industry matters as a longtime SAG member. She was involved in guild leadership and helped to steer some of the early SAG Awards ceremonies. In 1998, Fabares was supportive of early efforts to combine the Screen Actors Guild with the industry’s other major performers union, the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists. 

	After “Coach” ended its run, Fabares had few film and TV credits as she battled health problems. In 2000, she went through a very public health crisis in which she needed — and ultimately successfully received — a liver transplant. Her experience of waiting nearly two years for a donor liver to become available helped raise public awareness for the acute need for organ donations. Fabares was a longtime supporter of the Alzheimer’s Association, after her mother was diagnosed with the disease in the early 1990s.



	

					An Emmy FYC ad for “Coach” from the Feb. 9, 1991, edition of Daily Variety

schema.headline: Shelley Fabares, ‘Coach’ and ‘The Donna Reed Show’ Star, Dies at 82

title: ‘Boorman and the Devil’ Review: The Making of John Boorman’s 1977 Disaster ‘Exorcist II: The Heretic’ Becomes a Documentary So Unbelievable It’s Funny
description: “Boorman and the Devil” is a disaster movie that feels like a party. It’s a documentary about the making of one of the worst movies of its time, and
body:
“Boorman and the Devil” is a disaster movie that feels like a party. It’s a documentary about the making of one of the worst movies of its time, and maybe of all time — “Exorcist II: The Heretic,” the spectacularly misconceived and maladroit sequel to “The Exorcist.” It was a film so singular in its awfulness that when it came out in the summer of 1977, audiences laughed at it (they literally did), and the director, John Boorman, made a frantic attempt to recut it. (He lopped off the atrocious ending for a different atrocious ending.)
	

	Talented people can make terrible movies, and the era of “Exorcist II,” when directors still enjoyed the carte blanche that had come with the power of the New Hollywood, was littered with ambitious bombs, from Steven Spielberg’s “1941” to Peter Bogdanovich’s “At Long Last Love” to the granddaddy of them all, the stiff-necked but aimless three-and-a-half-hour Marxist art Western “Heaven’s Gate.” “Boorman and the Devil,” written and directed by David Kittredge, is a dishy and fascinating inside look at how one of the most legendary duds of the ’70s came to happen.


	Yet what lends the documentary its special, enjoyable flavor is that 50 years after “Exorcist II” was made, a number of the people connected with it, notably Boorman himself, still don’t fully grasp what the problem was. Boorman, seated in his wintry country home in County Wicklow, Ireland (he was 85 when the documentary was shot; he’s now 93), narrates the making of “Exorcist II” for us, and he still exudes a quality of shining belief in what he was doing. He made a movie so bad so that the audience felt no connection to it — but on some level of barely suppressed ego, he’s still blaming the audience for it. He thinks the film contains “some of the best work I’ve ever done.” He believes the problem is that the audience was expecting a different kind of movie. (Yes, a scary and not deathly boring one.)
	

	You might call Boorman’s fortitude admirable, but you could also call it delusional. And it lends “Boorman and the Devil” the quality of a true-life Christopher Guest film. For this is the unintentionally funny story of what happens when utterly unhinged and high-minded hubris becomes your guiding light. Boorman, and others associated with “Exorcist II,” know that they made an infamous disaster, yet the reason the film was a disaster still eludes them. The documentary is full of lines that, in context, have a double-edged drollery, as when the director Joe Dante says, “Many of the techniques that he uses, I’ve never seen repeated again!”

	Boorman thinks the problem with “Exorcist II” is that it failed to deliver the full-scale nasty horror blowout that the audience was expecting — and it’s true, that was a major problem. As Boorman acknowledges, this was all by design. After his success with “Deliverance” in 1972, Boorman had been offered the chance to direct “The Exorcist” (the original) but was repulsed by the book. “It seemed to me to be a book about torturing a child,” he says. “So I declined.” Three years later, when he was offered the sequel, Boorman said he wanted to make a movie that would be a mediation on the aftermath of “The Exorcist.” There’s no doubt that was his first mistake. No less a figure than Stanley Kubrick told him, “If you want to do a sequel to ‘The Exorcist,’ you just get more blood and gore.” This much was obvious.

	But the problem with “Exorcist II: The Heretic” wasn’t just that it failed to reconjure the primal terror and gruesome gross-out shock value of “The Exorcist.” It’s that the movie Boorman made instead was at once lifeless and preposterous. Boorman, who came up through the British new wave of the ’60s, had made several gripping thrillers that are recognized as classics — the tight, mean revenge noir “Point Blank” (1967) and then, of course, “Deliverance” (1972), the middle-class-friends-in-the-hillbilly-wilds thriller that established him as an A-list force in Hollywood. But Boorman, gifted as he was, had a flaky pretentious indulgent side; he was in thrall to third-rate “mythic” ideas. (He has remained so to this day.) Boorman passed on “The Exorcist” to make “Zardoz” (1974), a dystopian mess of spaced-out Jungian sci-fi, with Sean Connery running around in a Chippendale’s version of a bullet bandolier.
	

	It was this side of Boorman, the glittery-eyed “visionary” pedant, that enabled “Exorcist II.” The inspiration for the movie came from the French theologian Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, who believed that the human race was getting ready to come together into a kind of cosmic telepathic hive mind. “That piqued my interest,” says Boorman. “It was an opportunity to make a film about, really, metaphysics,” as well as “the next phase of human evolution.” “Exorcist II: The Heretic,” Boorman decided, would be a movie about synchronized hypnosis, with Linda Blair’s Regan trying to deal with the trauma of having had the devil inside her by sharing the experience with her therapist, Dr. Tuskin (Louise Fletcher), and with Father Philip Lamont (Richard Burton), the priest assigned by the Vatican to investigate what happened to Father Merrin.

	Here’s the thing about synchronized hypnosis. It’s one of those fruit-loop 1970s ideas — but more than that, it proved to be uniquely static as drama. “Exorcist II” turned out to be a movie about people sitting in a room staring at each other with wiry metal headbands on.

	The film’s folly extended to the one-note stentorian badness of Richard Burton’s performance, as he intoned such classy lines as “E-vil…is a spiritual being.” It extended to the ruinously expensive but still fakey-looking re-creation of Ethiopia on a soundstage, with piles of dirt being blown around by wind machines, enough arc lights to threaten to set the place on fire, and boulders that looked like they were made of Styrofoam. And it extended to the film’s weirdly abstract portrait of the devil, which would now be embodied by…locusts! Great teeming swarms of them, with an occasional locust seen in big buggy close-up, and shots of flying from a locust’s-eye view (the Steadicam had just been invented). It all looked like a cheesy disaster movie called “Attack of the Locusts” (in fact, a killer-bee movie called “The Swarm” came out a year later. Coincidence? Maybe not). James Earl Jones, as the African scientist Kokumo, donned a giant locust head like a Halloween costume and for some reason spit a whole tomato out of his mouth. Even the film’s name for the demon was ridiculous: Pazuzu. Every time you heard it, the more it sounded like baby talk.
	

	I saw “Exorcist II: The Heretic” the week it came out, and from the moment Linda Blair appeared, doing a smiley tap-dance for no good reason, through the orgy-of-destruction climax in what looked like a discotheque from hell, the film was staggering in its ineptitude. I left the theater shaking my head in disbelief. I had never seen it again until a year ago, and was unsurprised to discover that time had not been kind to it.

	Yet even as “Boorman and the Devil” gets you chortling at how the bad decisions piled up, the movie also sells the idea that Boorman was working on the high wire, and that “Exorcist II” was a folly with shades of greatness in it. Several notable critics are interviewed (they include Bilge Ebiri, Joseph McBride, and my friend Stephanie Zacharek), and they all testify to the idea that there’s some sort of loopy grandeur to what Boorman achieved. With all due respect, I think this is a complete fantasy, but it takes off from what Pauline Kael said about the movie at the time — that its imagery had a crazy spellbinding quality. Kael had hated “The Exorcist” (her despairing review of it is one of her greatest pieces — an example of how she could be a peerless critic even when you disagreed with her), and her kind comments about “Exorcist II” fit a pattern of hers where she would pan a film that became incredibly popular, then go on to embrace the far inferior sequel, almost as if it was her way of getting back in the loop. (She did this with “Exorcist II,” “Ghostbusters II,” and “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom.”)

	More to the point, in Kael’s comments on “Exorcist II,” you can hear the early stirrings of what would become Movie Disaster Rehabilitation Culture, which is now an industry among hipster cinephiles. Thus, the arid and didactic “Heaven’s Gate” has been elevated to the status of masterpiece. “Eyes Wide Shut,” which should have been about pedophilia (not aging swingers in masks), is now top-drawer Kubrick. And “Exorcist II” is a wacked but misunderstood grand folly. I passionately disagree with all three of those reassessments, and I think they’re all rooted in a certain impulse toward viewing movies in a postmodern way — as endlessly malleable texts rather than as stories that require an emotional logic and coherence that none of those films have. Wait long enough and even the worst movie, if it possesses the proper shoot-the-works ambition, can be “reframed.”
	

	“Boorman and the Devil” honors John Boorman’s ambition, but it also cuts him slack, notably when he’s saying things like, “In my experience, successful movies have one thing in common, and that’s luck.” What a load! What successful movies have in common — along with luck — is artists who know what they’re doing, and are rooted in the real world, and are working at the top of their game.

	That said, the making of “Exorcist II: The Heretic” was beset by a litany of bad decisions and bad luck, which piled up sky-high. Boorman got seriously ill with valley fever (from inhaling the imported dirt on set), and after he was hospitalized the production shut down for five weeks. The budget ballooned from $10 million to $15 million, making it the most expensive movie Warner Bros. had ever produced. Boorman and Rospo Pallenberg kept rewriting the script (because no one really knew what the movie was about), and Richard Burton was too dour and old and hungover. There was even an air of mishap surrounding the one sequence in the movie that’s truly effective — the dreamy moment where Regan balances on the edge of a rooftop with no railing. Boorman now acknowledges that the way they shot that scene (on the roof of the Warner Bros. building in New York), something could have gone very wrong.

	The story of the film’s first sneak preview, at a theater in Pasadena, with the Warner Bros. executives sitting nervously in the back of the theater, is a hilarious parable of the chickens coming home to roost. The audience sat there, dumbfounded at first, and then you started to hear the giggles; midway through, a man stood up and threatened the people who made the film, at which point they escaped. “Exorcist II” had been booked into 700 theaters for 12 weeks (a nearly unprecedented wide release at the time), but the attendance declined by 50 percent in the second weekend. The word had gotten out. All the recutting in the world couldn’t save it. “Boorman and the Devil,” in its amused way, does try to save “Exorcist II: The Heretic” by treating it as an insane work of artistic daring. But I’m sorry, that’s just a pile of Pazuzu.

title: Foo Fighters and Gustavo Dudamel Blow Up the Hollywood Bowl as Conductor Blows Out the Candle on His Time With the LA Phil: Concert Review
description:
The LA Phil has played with plenty of pop and rock acts before, but it may have taken Foo Fighters to really put the dude in Dudamel. 

	And not a m
body:
The LA Phil has played with plenty of pop and rock acts before, but it may have taken Foo Fighters to really put the dude in Dudamel. 

	And not a moment too soon, with this being famed conductor Gustavo Dudamel‘s final weekend at the helm of Los Angeles’ primary house symphony. The Phil’s hookup with Dave Grohl and company Saturday night was the middle act in a three-night local finale for Dudamel — a delectable dip into what old-school symphony buffs would once have considered low culture. The entire weekend, though, was about asking Beethoven to roll over, as it were, for some of the maestro’s less classical loves. The Foos collab was sandwiched in between Friday and Sunday concerts where the focus was on acknowledging Dudamel’s connections to Latin American and specifically Venezuelan music.
	

	Understandably, Grohl had to make it at least a little about himself, too, or more to the point, this being a milestone for his 32-year-old band. “ This is a first,” he told the sold-out crowd at the outset. “First of all, I don’t know if you know, but Foo Fighters has never played the Hollywood Bowl before… Usually in this part of the program I ask the audience if they love rock ‘n’ roll music… But tonight, i’m gonna ask this question for the first time: Do you love Dudamel? Me too. so let’s play some rock ‘n’ roll for Mr. Dudamel. That’s what we came here to do.”


	For a while, it seemed as if this show might really mark a serious first: Grohl, who tends to pepper his stage banter with the F-word at least once in every sentence — used as an exclamation, adjective, adverb, noun, verb and preposition — seemed to be inspired by the occasion, and by the presence of dozens of the world’s finest musicians in formalwear, to be deliberately abstaining from profanity. But if that was indeed a goal, finally, toward the end, he couldn’t help himself. “Ladies and gentlemen, on an evening like tonight, I don’t really know how to say goodbye, because I wish that we could do this every fucking night for the rest of our lives with all of these amazing people.”
	



	A quick, unscientific survey of Foo fans suggested that not one of them would have a problem with that (in, you know, the theoretical world where Grohl could outspend and out-prestige the New York Philharmonic, where Dudamel is headed next). Fans online — those who’d been at the concert and those just tracking it from afar — immediately began clamoring for a commercial release of Saturday’s show. That desire was well-justified. When some bands do symphonic hook-ups, it makes for a satisfying experiment, but not necessarily one you need to hear endlessly. The arrangements here were so well-balanced, and so in keeping with what made these tracks feel as dramatic as they did in the first place, that you could imagine recordings from the show taking the place of the originals in some fans’ streaming playlists, indefinitely if not for all time.

	Some artists who do Bowl shows with the LA Phil or its sister symphony, the Hollywood Bowl Orchestra, run through something close to their normal set and require whoever is assigned to do the orchestrations to follow suit. Fortunately, Grohl took a broader view of what catalog material might benefit most from the augmentation, even if it meant narrowing down the length of the setlist, since orchestral players by definition don’t work rock ‘n’ roll hours.

	“Listen, tonight we’re gonna play as many things as we can before we have to stop,” the singer said early in the hour-and-40-minutes performance. “You know, we usually play for three hours a night. But tonight, we picked the best songs that we could perform with our friends in the LA Phil and Mr. Gustavo Dudamel. Some of these you may have never heard before. So sit back and enjoy a song called ‘A320.'”



	

					Foo Fighters and Gustavo Dudamel (third from left) take a bow at the close of Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA, at the Hollywood Bowl August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic
	



	Now, pretty much the only people who’ve been holding out for “A320” to rejoin the Foos’ set after a quarter-century of absence are the half-dozen people still clutching to their CDs of the 1998 “Godzilla” soundtrack, where it first lived and kind of died a quiet death. But, as one of the rare songs to have included string arrangements on the original record, it was prime territory for revival here. (And the band has also been trying it out at a few non-orchestral tour stops this year, maybe with the thought of getting it ready for the Bowl.) As on the age-old original, the first half of the six-minute track was sweeping in its use of orchestral augmentation, and then the second half put aside both strings and vocals to turn into a pure band jam. That’s counterintuitive, since it would be more common to start a song without orchestration and then add it in, rather than the reverse. But the band fury is as climactic as anything that could be done continuing to have the full ensemble play… and Dudamel looked happy enough to put his baton down, turn around and just watch the group play for a few minutes. (The Phil was present at points on every one of the 15 songs song, but there were plenty of stretches within those songs where they took five.)
	



	

					HB26 Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA – August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic
	



	The band’s most faithful followers may be happy to hear “Times Like These” played for the 894th time (according to setlist.fm), but having “A320” come into the set early was a sign that this would really be a night to make the hardcore happy. And there ended up being three more rarities to set fans aflutter: “I Should Have Known,” being played live for the first time since 2012; “Razor,” being performed for the first time since 2006; and “Home,” getting a live airing for the first time since 2007 (and only the fifth performance overall). What these surprise additions meant, in human terms, is that Grohl understood the assignment, when it came to joining forces with another powerful institution: you find the songs that have been waiting for that moment.

	Of course, he also considered some of the band’s greatest hits to be in that category. “This was made for the Hollywood Bowl, I think,” Grohl said, prefacing “My Hero.” It was hard to argue with that assessment, when the song took on a healthy dose of brass that sounded noble enough for a military funeral… not to mention a surprise solo harp for just a few seconds when the rest of the onstage complement dropped out for a dramatic pause. 

	But it really was some of the lesser known or slightly less celebrated songs making bigger impressions. A choir came out on two songs in the middle of the set, both of them highlights. First among them was “The Sky Is a Neighborhood” (the title of which lets you know that Grohl does have a poetic side, however much his stage banter falls into the category of basic-bitch). The frontman did some of his punkiest scream-singing of the night, content to know that the dozen or so berobed figures surrounding him could keep up the melodious quotient of the tune; Chris Shiflett turned in a short, sweet and rare guitar solo over some of that choral wailing, as the band thunderously pounded it out in 6/8 time. Maximalism doesn’t come much more maximal than that, and it was genuinely musical as well as bombastic. 



	

					HB26 Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA – August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic
	



	Then, taking it way down, members of the participating YOLA (the Youth Orchestra of Los Angeles), identifiable by their shirts (and by their, duh, youth), did a somber string opening for “Run,” replicating or replacing the studio version’s extended acoustic guitar intro, before the rock and the choir kicked in — another certain highlight, despite the tune not being on the list of internationally approved classics.
	

	More expected standouts included “Aurora,” which Grohl has been faithfully dedicating nightly to Taylor Hawkins, with the orchestra again going silent during the final stretch so that the core band could use the hypnotically interesting riffage to send a former comrade into the afterlife with 17,000 phones aglow. 

	It didn’t seem as if it would get much more sentimental than that, yet it did, as the unlikely penultimate pick turned out to be “Home,” of which Grohl said, “We’ve only done this song once.” (He was off-count by about three instances, according to the online stats, but close enough.) Taking a stool for the most sedate of his ballads, Grohl explained that he was never previously able to get through the 2007 song “because it’s such a meaningful song to me that whenever I heard it, I couldn’t stop from crying. And whenever we played it, there’s no way I could make it through the entire song without just bursting into tears. But what I’ve found is that while you’re singing it, if you think of other things, you can actually make it to the end without crying.” There was a pause, while the audience waited for Grohl to explain if he was picturing the audience naked, or something. “I’m not gonna tell you what I was thinking about,” he then announced. “But we got to the end of the fucking song, so there you go.”

	There might have been other reasons to wonder whether Grohl would make it through the set, early on — like, right, at the very beginning, when the set started with a slow and stark couple of verses of “Times Like These,” and the singer’s voice cracked when he sang that high, introductory “I…” And the same thing happened when that note came around again. Was it an inauspicious way to start the set, revealing a voice that was tour-ravaged… or was Grohl faking us out with some exaggerated emotion? Whichever was the case, he quickly rallied, or otherwise revved up to speed, and there were no worries about whether his howl would survive this hot night from then on. But he had us going for about half a minute there. 

	A good thing he turned out to deceptively be in top shape after all; this will go down in many fans’ books as one of the group’s all-timers. Whether the show is memorialized through some sort of commemorative recording or just cameraphone videos, it’s some of the little things that stick in memory, at least initially: the way that the horns filled in the space between the lines of verses on “All My Life” with frenetic stabs, or how, on “Learn to Fly,” the strings played slightly off the beat in the dramatic coda, versus the straightforward slamming of the band. And the fake endings … so many fake endings. But Grohl is showman enough to know: when a fast song leaves ’em wanting more, it doesn’t hurt to seem to quit and then actually give a little more.
	

	Dudamel did not do much talking; if he has any sentimental feelings he wants to share with the L.A. audience about taking leave of them, presumably he will do it during Sunday night’s true swan song. But he did speak while introducing what amounted to the evening’s opening act — a 15-minute border-crossing suite, composer Aldemaro Romero’s “Fuga con Pajarillo,” which segued back and forth between the full orchestra and Venezuelan musicians, including Eduardo Betancourt, Jorge Glem and Moisés Torrealba. The main reason for the night was, as Grohl said, “to give Gustavo one more big rock show before he has to leave this wonderful city.” But even then, he couldn’t leave Venezuela out of it. New York will be blessed to have someone so faithful to his truest loves.

	Which definitely do include rock. Dudamel’s performance conducting with Foo Fighters Saturday made you wish the LA Phil, or future employers, would dedicate one of the venue’s big screens solely to a Gustavo Cam, so everyone could see how headbanging really should look, when it’s being done by a pro.



	

					Dave Grohl and conductor Gustavo Dudamel perform as part of Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA – August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic
	



	Setlist for Foo Fighters with the LA Phil, Gustavo Dudamel and YOLA at the Hollywood Bowl, August 22, 2026:Times Like These All My LifeThe PretenderWalkA320 My HeroLearn to FlyThe Sky Is a NeighborhoodRunI Should Have KnownRazor AuroraBest of YouHomeEverlong



	

					Gustvavo Dudamel with Venezuelan musicians backstage at Celebrating Gustavo at the Bowl: Foo Fighters with the LA Phil and YOLA – August 22, 2026
									Timothy Norris/Los Angeles Philharmonic

title: Grace Passô’s ‘Our Secret’ Nabs the Best Film Kikito at the 54th Gramado Film Festival
description: GRAMADO, Brazil — “Our Secret” (“Nosso segredo”), the first feature from Grace Passô, nabbed the best feature film Kikito award at the Aug. 22 closi
body:
GRAMADO, Brazil — “Our Secret” (“Nosso segredo”), the first feature from Grace Passô, nabbed the best feature film Kikito award at the Aug. 22 closing ceremony of the 54th Gramado Film Festival. The feature also scooped cinematography (Wilssa Esser) and art direction (Lucas Osório) plaudits.

	Passô, an established playwright and also actress, directed and wrote the feature that tells the story of a Black family trying to rebuild its routine after a recent loss. As family members avoid grief, the youngest son keeps a secret that may lead them to confront the roots of their pain.
	

	Vitrine Filmes, the distributor of Kleber Mendonça Filho’s “The Secret Agent,” will release “Our Secret” in local theaters Aug. 27.




	

					‘Gugu’s World’ 
									Courtesy of Gramado Film Festival
	



	Allan Deberton’s “Gugu’s World” (“Feito Pipa”) took home the audience award, plus director, actress (Teca Pereira) and supporting actor (Lázaro Ramos) Kikitos.

	Carlos Segundo’s “Milk Powder” () walked off with the critics’ jury award for Brazilian feature film, screenplay (Segundo and Rafael Copel) and sound design (Waldir Xavier).

	In the acting categories, José Loreto, for “Chorão: Só os Loucos Sabem,” and Christian Malheiros, for “Justino: Nos Bastidores do Reino,” shared the actor prize. Naruna Costa, for “Pele de Rinoceronte,” nabbed the supporting actress Kikito. The jury granted honorable mentions for 11-year-old Yuri Gomes (“Gugu’s World”) and Onna Silva (“Justino: Nos Bastidores do Reino”).

	André Finotti and José Eduardo Belmonte took the editing Kikito for “Justino: Nos Bastidores do Reino” and Otávio de Moraes received the original score award for “Chorão: Só os Loucos Sabem.”
	

	Susanna Lira’s “Gonzaguinha, da Maior Liberdade” won the doc feature Kikito, while “Empeleitada” received an honorable mention in the doc category.

	The jury was comprised of actress Cris Vianna, director and screenwriter Fábio Meira, actress Helena Ranaldi, researcher, film critic and curator Kênia Freitas and actor Marcelo Serrado.

	The critics’ jury consisted of journalist and doc filmmaker Flavia Guerra, journalist and professor Pâmela Eurídice, doc filmmaker and critic Rafael Valles, journalist and director Simone Zuccolotto and researcher and critic Victor Souza.

	During the fest, actor Marcos Caruso received the Troféu Cidade de Gramado; producer Renata Almeida Magalhães was honored with the Troféu Eduardo Abelin; Selton Mello and Maria Fernanda Cândido accepted the Troféu Kikito de Cristal; and Andrea Beltrão took the Troféu Oscarito.

	Gramado Fest winners:

	Best Film: “Our Secret,” by Grace Passô

	Best Documentary Feature: “Gonzaguinha, da Maior Liberdade,” by Susanna Lira

	Documentary Honorable Mention: “Empeleitada”

	Audience Award for Best Film: “Gugu’s World,” by Allan Deberton

	Critics’ Jury Award for Best Film: “Milk Powder” (“Leite em Pó”) by Carlos Segundo

	Best Director: Allan Deberton for “Gugu’s World”

	Best Actress: Teca Pereira for “Gugu’s World”

	Best Actor: José Loreto for “Chorão: Só os Loucos Sabem” and Christian Malheiros for “Justino: Nos Bastidores do Reino”

	Honorable Mention: Yuri Gomes for “Gugu’s World”

	Honorable Mention: Onna Silva for “Justino: Nos Bastidores do Reino”

	Best Screenplay: Carlos Segundo and Rafael Copel for “Milk Powder”

	Best Cinematography: Wilssa Esser for “Our Secret”

	Best Supporting Actor: Lázaro Ramos for “Gugu’s World”

	Best Supporting Actress: Naruna Costa for “Pele de Rinoceronte”

	Best Sound Design: Waldir Xavier for “Milk Powder”

	Best Original Score: Otávio de Moraes for “Chorão: Só os Loucos Sabem”

	Best Art Direction: Lucas Osório for “Our Secret”

	Best Editing: André Finotti and José Eduardo Belmonte for “Justino: Nos Bastidores do Reino”

title: Buckcherry Tour Bus Crash Involved Three Separate Accidents, Highway Patrol Says
description:
Buckcherry Tour Bus Crash
                          Three Separate Accidents Involved in Fatal Wr
body:
Buckcherry Tour Bus Crash
                          Three Separate Accidents Involved in Fatal Wreck
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Rock band Buckcherry's tour bus was caught up in a chaotic chain of three separate accidents on a South Carolina highway, which ended fatal, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            South Carolina Highway Patrol spokesperson tells TMZ the series of crashes unfolded one after another. According to cops, the first accident was a single-car crash involving a male driver. Investigators are still trying to determine what caused him to crash.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The situation turned deadly moments later when the man got out of his vehicle and was struck by another motorist. The man was killed in the collision.
      

            Police tell TMZ the driver who struck and killed the man was not arrested, and the circumstances surrounding that collision remain under investigation. Then, moments later, a third crash occurred -- this time involving Buckcherry's tour bus.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told the bus was involved in a whopping five-vehicle crash, with some people involved suffered minor injuries, but no one was taken to the hospital. The cause of that third collision is also under investigation.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The new details clarify the circumstances surrounding our previous report of Buckcherry's bus being involved in a fatal multi-vehicle crash. The band's members and touring crew were safe and unharmed, the band announced Friday.
      
    
            The band is currently on tour and has continued its scheduled performances following the crash. The man who was killed has not been publicly identified.
      
    
                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            The investigations into all three accidents remain ongoing.
